title: Chipping at the Gates
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · Reading an argument, choosing words
objective: Students will read the exhibition’s poster *The Writing Revolution* as an argument rather than a list of facts. They will trace its claim, its evidence, the challenges it admits and the question it leaves open; notice how strong verbs such as *shattered*, *obliterated* and *chipped away* and the metaphor of gates shape the reader’s view; and see, at the Typing Station, how a typewriter and a computer change the way a writer revises.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every argument you read was built from choices. Seeing those choices lets you agree, disagree, and build your own.

items.text: identify the claim, evidence and complications in a nonfiction argument
items.question: find the claim, the evidence and the complications in the poster?

items.text: explain how a writer’s word choice, such as *shattered* and *obliterated*, shapes a reader’s view
items.question: explain how words like shattered and obliterated shape what you think?

items.text: describe how the tools of writing change the way a writer revises
items.question: describe how a typewriter and a computer change the way you revise?

items.text: write a short argument that answers the poster’s question about AI writing tools, with a counterclaim
items.question: write your own argument about AI writing tools, with a counterclaim?

materials: The argument map on page 3, projected or printed
The poster *The Writing Revolution*, on screen at the exhibition or printed
The Typing Station on the exhibition website, for the revision demonstration
Differentiated handouts, one per student; pens
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** read *The Writing Revolution* aloud, listening for its verbs. Then at the Typing Station, type the same line on the typewriter and on the iMac, and notice what you do differently when a mistake cannot be erased.

steps.title: Words that break
script: Put three sentences from the poster on the screen without comment: *“This exclusivity shattered with each technological leap.”* *“The computer age obliterated remaining barriers.”* *“Every new technology has chipped away at the gates that once kept most voices silent.”* Ask: *“Which words describe breaking something?”* Collect *shattered*, *obliterated*, *chipped away*. Ask what each one makes the reader feel about the old way of writing.

screen.text:
This exclusivity shattered with each technological leap.
The computer age obliterated remaining barriers.
Every new technology has chipped away at the gates that once kept most voices silent.

steps.purpose: Notice the language before the facts: the poster’s verbs are verbs of breaking.
students: Why might a writer choose them?

steps.title: The argument map
script: Show the argument map on page 3. Name each move: the **claim** (writing was a privilege, and that exclusivity *shattered*), the **evidence** (a technology at each step), the **complication** (*Yet this power brings new challenges: information overload, the spread of misinformation, and algorithms that decide what writing gets seen.*), the **open question** about AI, and the **conclusion** about the gates.
Ask why a writer would admit problems with their own argument. Introduce the term **concession**: granting a point that seems to work against you, which can make an argument more trustworthy.

screen.caption: How The Writing Revolution builds its argument

cells: For thousands of years, writing was a privilege reserved for scribes, monks, and the wealthy elite. This exclusivity shattered with each technological leap.
The printing press around 1440; the typewriter in 1868; word processors in the 1970s; PageMaker in 1985; Blogger in 1999 and Wikipedia in 2001.
Yet this power brings new challenges: information overload, the spread of misinformation, and algorithms that decide what writing gets seen.
As AI writing tools emerge, we face the ultimate democratization—what happens when anyone can generate professional-quality text instantly?
Every new technology has chipped away at the gates that once kept most voices silent.

steps.purpose: See the poster as an argument: a claim, evidence, a complication, an open question, a conclusion.
students: Why would a writer admit problems with their own argument?

steps.title: Two ways to revise
script: Open the Typing Station. On the typewriter there is no erasing: Back space strikes over. On the iMac, students can select, cut and paste, change the font and undo. Read: *“Early word processors in the 1970s meant anyone could edit and perfect their writing without costly reprints.”* Ask: *how does the tool change the way you revise?*

screen.alt: The Typing Station room: a typewriter on the coral wall, its first line typed on the sheet of paper, with the tabs Typewriter, iMac, Top row and Class Board
screen.caption: The Typing Station: the same line on a typewriter and on an iMac

steps.purpose: Connect the poster’s claim about word processors to how students revise.
students: On the typewriter, a mistake stays on the page. On the iMac, Back space takes it away.
Which machine would make you a better reviser?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the same poster; each ends with writing of their own.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find the breaking words and say why a writer chose them, sort sentences by their job in the argument, and write a short answer to *what would you publish?*

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Map the argument in their own words, weigh four strong words against plainer ones, and draft by typewriter rules before revising.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge whether the poster’s concessions strengthen it, examine its metaphors, and write an argument answering its question about AI, with a counterclaim.

steps.purpose: Read the poster’s argument and write back to it at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the same poster.

steps.title: One word
script: Ask: *“Which single word in the poster does the most work? Why that one?”* Take several answers; have a Red Level student read the opening of their AI argument aloud.

screen.question: Which single word in the poster does the most work? Why that one?

steps.purpose: Bring the lesson’s two strands together: a single choice of word carries an argument.
students: Point to the sentence it is in.
What would change if the writer had chosen a plainer word?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
steps.purpose: Check what each student can now do against the objectives.
